title: It Correlates. So What?
scopeNote: This keeps the correlation model and the live regression that produces an incremental validity figure, cut to four measures and one control. The ability-based measure, the shared-method controls, the six-measure matrix and the set of marketing claims to judge stay in the longer version.
summary: A fictional new questionnaire correlates around 0.4 with the outcome at every setting of one control, while what it adds beyond the measures already available falls from ten percentage points of explained variance to almost nothing.
learningObjectives: Explain why a correlation with an outcome is a weaker claim than adding something new.
Define incremental validity and say what it is measured against.
Explain why a measure that overlaps an existing one can still correlate well with the outcome.
Recognise that modest overlap is not by itself an objection to a measure.
Say what a decision-maker would need to know before adopting a new measure.
interactionTypes: a judgement about what a replicated correlation establishes
a live control over how much a new measure overlaps an existing one
the correlation with the outcome and the incremental contribution recomputed together
two lines whose behaviour across the range is opposite
a guided setting in which the new measure is largely an existing one renamed
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. No questionnaire is administered and nothing is inferred about the learner.
dataStatus: Four fictional descriptions of method types. No published emotional-intelligence measure is reproduced, quoted, paraphrased or scored, no number is an estimate of any real quantity, and the page takes no position on whether emotional intelligence exists.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with overlap on a native range input reporting its value in text. Every figure in the chart is also a readout tile, and the three measures' correlations are in a real table with row and column headers, so the lines are never the only route to the numbers. Each line is labelled by name at its end rather than distinguished by colour, and the tile reporting what the measure adds states the meaning in words and carries a non-colour state signal. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
simulationNotes: Each measure is a weighted sum of independent standard normal sources scaled to unit variance, so the implied correlation between two of them is the sum of the products of their shared coefficients. The outcome loads on a dispositional source, a source specific to handling feelings and a general cognitive one; the personality questionnaire loads on the first alone and the reasoning test on the third alone, so the two comparison measures are uncorrelated and the base model is a clean sum of two squared correlations. The single control sets the new questionnaire's dispositional loading, with its feelings-specific loading following from holding the sum of their squares fixed, so the measure carries the same total amount of outcome-relevant content at every setting and only its composition changes. The result is that its correlation with the outcome stays between 0.36 and 0.48 while what it adds beyond the two existing measures falls from about 10.1 percentage points of explained variance to about 0.3, a more than thirtyfold collapse; the increment falls monotonically and the raw correlation does not, so the advertised figure cannot be read back to the overlap. The control's range is deliberate: incremental validity is robust to modest overlap and collapses only when the overlap is large, which is a real property of the arithmetic rather than something to engineer away, and a slider spanning the whole space would spend most of its travel doing nothing. The synthesis says in as many words that substantial overlap is not by itself an objection. Simplifications, all stated: population values with no sampling error, where real incremental validity is poorly estimated at the usual sample sizes; a comparison set chosen for the learner, when incremental validity is always relative to it; and prediction treated as the only reason to prefer a measure, which it is not.
readmeTopic: why a measure correlating with an outcome does not mean it is worth having
